Adopt Vectorized HURRECON Over CLIMADA for Puerto Rico Wind Hazard Mapping

Evaluating HURRECON's closed-form parametric equations directly on the projected 250 m EPSG:32161 grid inside ArcGIS Pro's native Python 3.13.13 runtime preserves 1955–2025 IBTrACS provenance, models land-water friction across all four islands, and avoids CLIMADA v6.2.0's Mamba environment overhead and pre-1980 pressure imputation traps.

71 yrs

Unbroken 1955–2025 North Atlantic observation eligibility under HURRECON using USA_LAT, USA_LON, and USA_WIND across 1,143 storms (62,485 prepared points), without requiring central pressure or historical radius records.

Primary Decision: Native HURRECON

Implement the published HURRECON radial wind and friction equations directly against your 304,380 reference grid centroids using ArcGIS Pro's bundled numpy and arcpy. This eliminates intermediate lat/lon GeoTIFF reprojection and satisfies the Boose, Serrano, & Foster (2004) Puerto Rico calibration standard.

CLIMADA v6.2.0 Python 3.13 Reality

Although CLIMADA v6.2.0 installation docs expanded Allowed Versions to 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 (keeping 3.11 as the primary Supported Version), CLIMADA still cannot be installed via pip alone and requires a separate conda-forge Mamba environment that breaks turnkey ArcGIS Pro ModelBuilder portability.

Right-Sized 1–3–5 Classification

Map annual hurricane-force (≥64 kt / 33 m/s) exceedance frequency λ64 = N64 / 71 into Low (1), Medium (3), and High (5) using Boose et al. (2004) recurrence intervals, paired with a frozen island-wide tertile sensitivity check matching your Drought workflow.

CLIMADA v6.2.0 Allows Python 3.13, Yet Still Requires Environment Isolation

Your note in hurricane_processing_plan.md was written against CLIMADA v6.1.0 documentation, which listed Python 3.11 as Supported and 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 as Allowed—creating a hard version-number conflict with ArcGIS Pro 3.7's bundled Python 3.13.13.

In the latest release, CLIMADA v6.2.0 (updated installation matrix), ETH Zurich kept Python 3.11 as the tested Supported Version but shifted Allowed Versions to 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 (dropping 3.10). Update your processing plan to reflect that Python 3.13 is now an allowed interpreter version, while retaining the separate-environment requirement for three concrete technical reasons.

Mamba Solver Requirement

The CLIMADA installation guide explicitly warns that its compiled dependencies (cartopy, rasterio, h5py, numba, pyproj, netcdf4, dask) cannot be installed with pip alone and require mamba create -n climada_env -c conda-forge with nodefaults.

ArcGIS Pro ABI Integrity

Forcing conda-forge geospatial binaries into ArcGIS Pro's arcgispro-py3 environment (or a cloned Pro environment) conflicts with Esri's pinned gdal, proj, and arcpy C++ bindings. Worse, classmates grading or running your HurricaneWinds_Model_Toolbox.atbx in ArcGIS Pro cannot execute a ModelBuilder graph that shells out to an unbundled Mamba environment.

pyproject.toml Lag

While the ReadTheDocs matrix lists 3.13 as allowed, the upstream CLIMADA pyproject.toml and conda-forge solver constraints still recommend python=3.11.* in advanced installs to prevent dependency solver deadlocks across binary wheels.

Recommended text update for docs/hurricane_processing_plan.md:
"CLIMADA v6.2.0 retains Python 3.11 as its primary supported version and expands allowed versions to 3.11–3.13 (replacing v6.1.0's 3.10–3.12 range). Although Python 3.13.13 in ArcGIS Pro 3.7 is now within CLIMADA's allowed version range, CLIMADA still requires a dedicated Mamba/conda-forge environment (climada_env) that cannot be installed via pip or merged safely into arcgispro-py3."

Head-to-Head Comparison Favors HURRECON Across Fidelity, Coverage, and Scope

The course assignment requires transforming raw IBTrACS observations into a reproducible 250 m ranked raster (Low = 1, Medium = 3, High = 5) inside an executable ArcGIS Pro ModelBuilder workflow. While prior course examples (such as Variable Index Calculation Process Example.txt) simply buffered or reclassified raw vector lines, Section 3 of the Fall 2026 syllabus explicitly prohibits naive point/line rasterization: "Use a justified model, interpolation, or density method when estimating a continuous surface. Rasterizing observations alone does not estimate unobserved locations."

Physics and Spatial Mechanics: Why HURRECON Captures Puerto Rico's Landfall Gradient

Atlantic hurricanes approaching Puerto Rico typically track west-northwest, placing the northeastern quadrant of the island (Luquillo Mountains, Fajardo, Vieques, and Culebra) in the storm's right-front quadrant where forward translation speed Vh adds constructively to cyclonic rotation (Boose et al., 2004). Once the vortex crosses the coastline, surface roughness over land reduces sustained 10 m wind speed by approximately 20% (F = 0.8) and increases the cross-isobar inflow angle from 20° (water) to 40° (land).

HURRECON Closed-Form Governing Equations

As documented in Boose, Serrano, & Foster (2004) and the HurreconPython specification, the 1-minute sustained surface wind speed Vs at any grid cell center P at distance R > 0 from the storm center in the Northern Hemisphere is:

Vs(P) = F · [ Vm − S · (1 − sin T) · Vh / 2 ] · √( (Rmw / R)B · exp(1 − (Rmw / R)B) )

Here Vm is the IBTrACS USA_WIND (converted from knots to m/s via 1 kt = 0.514444 m/s, or kept in knots consistently), Vh is the forward translation speed derived from consecutive rebuilt USA_LAT/USA_LON positions, T is the clockwise angle from the storm forward heading to cell P (peaking at T = 90° on the right side where 1 − sin T = 0, and reducing wind by S · Vh on the left side at T = 270° with S = 1.0), Rmw is the radius of maximum winds, and B (s_par) is the Holland-type radial profile exponent.

CLIMADA H08 Pressure–Wind Formulation

By contrast, CLIMADA's default TropCyclone H08 solver (Holland, 2008) derives bs as a function of central pressure deficit Δp = pn − pc, latitude φ, pressure tendency &partial;pc/&partial;t, and translational speed vt:

bs = −4.4×10−5Δp2 + 0.01Δp + 0.03(&partial;pc/&partial;t) − 0.014φ + 0.15vtx + 1.0

While theoretically sophisticated for modern aircraft-reconnaissance storms, Holland (2008) himself notes that North Atlantic archives between 1950 and 1980 have severe central-pressure gaps and Dvorak wind-pressure biases. When USA_PRES is missing in IBTrACS, CLIMADA must synthetically regress pressure from wind before computing the radial profile—introducing hidden double-approximation without applying land friction (F = 0.8) over Puerto Rico.

Historical Data Completeness Makes HURRECON the Only Non-Imputed 1955–2025 Engine

Your prepared geodatabase (hurricane_prepare.gdb/hurricane_observations) retains 62,485 main-track observations across 1,143 North Atlantic storms from 1955 through 2025. As established in your preparation contract, "A prepared record's existence does not authorize an engine to turn missing pressure, radius, or wind into a calm field."

In the NOAA IBTrACS v04r01 archive, USA_LAT, USA_LON, and USA_WIND are populated across nearly the entire 1955–2025 record. By contrast, central pressure (USA_PRES) is frequently absent prior to systematic satellite/reconnaissance standardization in 1979 (Holland, 2008), and NHC best-track wind radii (USA_R34/50/64) and USA_RMW were only systematically archived in best-track reanalyses starting in 2004 (Chen et al., 2024).

Right-Sizing the Intermediate Pipeline: Avoid Over-Engineering While Preserving 250 m Grid Fidelity

A common trap in student GIS projects is either under-engineering (buffering storm tracks by an arbitrary distance, which violates Section 3 of your course assignment) or over-engineering (spinning up external Conda environments, writing thousands of temporary geographic GeoTIFFs to disk via standalone HurreconPython, and running arcpy.management.ProjectRaster 1,143 times). Because HURRECON's physical equation is closed-form and vectorizable in numpy, you can execute the exact Boose et al. (2004) model directly on your existing 250 m EPSG:32161 grid inside a single ArcPy Script Tool.

Stage A: Candidate Track Screen & 15-Min Sub-Stepping

Retain full storm tracks from hurricane_prepare.gdb/hurricane_observations, filter to storms passing within a conservative 350 km bounding radius of the Puerto Rico study envelope (roughly 120–160 candidate storms out of 1,143), and linearly interpolate 3–6 hourly observations to 15-minute time steps so fast-moving storms (e.g., Hugo 1989, Maria 2017) never skip over island cells between synoptic timestamps.

Stage B: Direct Centroid Evaluation in EPSG:32161

Instead of generating lat/lon rasters in external HurreconPython and resampling them, pre-compute the WGS84 coordinates (or EPSG:32161 meters) of the active land cells (mask == 1, roughly 145,000 land pixels out of 304,380 total cells). Evaluate the HURRECON equation in vectorized NumPy arrays with F = 0.8 (land), S = 1.0, baseline Rmw = 30 km (or observed USA_RMW where valid in sensitivity runs), and B = 1.4 (Boose et al., 2004).

Stage C: Validation Gate & 1–3–5 Raster Publication

Verify reconstructed peak wind footprints for Hurricane Maria (2017) and Hurricane Georges (1998) against NHC recorded USA_R64 / USA_R34 quadrant radii and Van Beusekom et al. (2018) 250 m disturbance maps. Accumulate the 71-season exceedance count N64(c), compute λ64(c) = N64(c) / 71, and reclassify directly to HurricaneWinds_rank250.tif with valid integer ranks 1, 3, 5 and exterior NoData.

Peer-Reviewed Literature Evidence Matrix for Section 2 of the Course Report

Your course syllabus (Section 2, Page 2) requires an evidence matrix examining at least two peer-reviewed research articles for Hurricane Winds (five total across your two variables; your drought_processing_plan.md already supplies five for Drought) and asks you to cite 1–3 literature articles to justify the physical indicator and the three risk/hazard classes (Low = 1, Medium = 3, High = 5). The four peer-reviewed articles below provide complete coverage of the HURRECON model, the CLIMADA/Holland alternative, 250 m Puerto Rico validation, and return-period classification thresholds.

doi:10.1890/02-4057		 Puerto Rico archipelago (1508–1997; 43 hurricanes since 1851 from HURDAT); regional reconstruction at 500 m to 3 km, plus 30 m topographic exposure in Luquillo. Classifies sustained wind into modified Fujita classes: F0 (18–32 m/s / 35–63 kt, tropical-storm force), F1 (33–49 m/s / 64–96 kt, Cat 1–2 hurricane), F2 (50–69 m/s / 97–134 kt, major hurricane), F3+ (≥70 m/s). Calibrated on 7 modern PR hurricanes with station wind observations and validated independently against municipal damage reports for 36 historical PR storms. Direct primary precedent for both our HURRECON engine and our 3-class recurrence thresholds across Puerto Rico.

Justifying the 3 Classes of Risk Index Scores (Low = 1, Medium = 3, High = 5)

Unlike the simplified course example (Variable Index Calculation Process Example.txt) that assigned arbitrary 1 / 5 / 10 scores to vector hurricane lines, your Fall 2026 assignment requires exact Low = 1, Medium = 3, and High = 5 integer scores on the 250 m grid, asks you to "distinguish thresholds taken directly from a source from adaptations you propose," and mandates testing "at least one alternative set of thresholds or aggregation rule and report how much land changes class."

To satisfy both requirements rigorously without over-complicating your ModelBuilder workflow, define the physical indicator at each valid 250 m land cell c over the Y = 71 seasons (1955–2025) as the annual hurricane-force exceedance rate λ64(c) = N64(c) / 71 (with empirical mean return interval T64(c) = 71 / N64(c) years), where N64(c) is the number of distinct storms whose modeled HURRECON peak sustained surface wind at cell c reaches at least 64 kt (32.92 m/s, corresponding to both the NOAA Saffir-Simpson Category 1 threshold and the Boose et al., 2004 F1 structural/forest damage threshold of 33 m/s). Then evaluate the three classification rules below:
